intro: VialGrade is a research site I built to compare peptide vendors and check the evidence behind their claims.
orientation: A friend of mine is really into biomedicine and peptide research. He told me people around him were buying peptides, but a lot of the vendors seemed sketchy, so I started looking at the sites myself.
origin: Every site seemed to say the same things: third-party tested, verified certificates, high purity. There would be a document on the page, but I didn't know whether it actually belonged to that batch or company. I wanted a better way to compare the claims than just take the website's word for it.

I started building VialGrade around those checks. A certificate of analysis, or COA, is a lab report. The site brings together lab records and batch information so someone can see what lines up, what doesn't, and where the evidence came from.
unknown: One thing I had to figure out was what to do when there wasn't enough information. Not finding a lab record doesn't tell me that the vendor did something wrong. I didn't want the software to give someone a bad grade just because I hadn't collected enough data on them, so it can return no grade at all.
grading: The grade looks beyond one certificate, at independent testing and things like regulatory records and information about the business. A documented problem can still pull it down even when other records look good. The grade is about the evidence I have, not a guarantee about what's in a vial.
handoff: I originally wanted checkout on VialGrade, but I couldn't make that work. The site links to the vendor instead, which meant I also needed a way to see whether those links were being used.
attribution: I added tracking tags and a short VialGrade click reference to the links. I can track the handoff and the destination can identify where the traffic came from, although that still doesn't tell me whether someone bought anything.
earlyUse: In an early update, I'd recorded about 2,000 Google impressions, around 600 clicks into the site, and eight signups over a month. That honestly surprised me. It was still small, but people I didn't know were finding it and using it.
takeaway: What I wanted was one place to look at a vendor's claim and actually follow it back to something. There's a lot the site can't establish, and I want that to be visible too.
